title: Breast cancer — lump → triple assessment → management
scenario: A 60-year-old lady comes to your clinic complaining of changes in her breast (picture). 438A · Archive A 50-year-old woman with a mass in the right breast and axilla; US done. 436F
A 50-year-old lady with a painless breast lump. 437A
A 45-year-old woman with a breast mass; nothing significant on history & exam. 441F
A case of triple-negative breast cancer. 441A

imgs.cap: Locally advanced breast cancer — skin changes, ulceration/fungating mass

qs.q: What do you see?
a: Skin changes (erythema, ulceration/fungating lesion, peau d'orange, tethering) and a breast mass.
qs.why: Skin involvement (ulceration, peau d'orange from blocked dermal lymphatics, tethering) with a mass means a locally advanced breast cancer.

qs.q: Take a history.
a: Lump: onset, size change, pain, relation to cycle; nipple discharge/retraction, skin changes; axillary lump.

Risk factors: age, family history (BRCA), early menarche/late menopause, nulliparity/late first pregnancy, no breastfeeding, HRT/OCP, previous breast disease/radiation, obesity, alcohol. Constitutional & metastatic symptoms (bone pain, SOB, headache, jaundice).
qs.why: The history characterises the lump, looks for local spread (skin, nipple, axilla) and metastatic symptoms, and scores risk (hormonal exposure, family history/BRCA).
hist: Rapid growth suggests malignancy; slow or no change is more benign.
Cyclical change suggests fibrocystic (benign) disease; most cancers are painless.
Bloody discharge or new retraction raise suspicion of cancer.
Peau d'orange, dimpling or ulceration suggest locally advanced cancer.
Early menarche, late menopause, nulliparity, late first pregnancy, no breastfeeding, HRT/OCP
Previous breast disease or radiation, obesity, alcohol
Symptoms of metastases to bone, lung, brain and liver — change staging and treatment.

qs.q: What will you do? / How would you diagnose her?
a: Triple assessment: history & examination + imaging (mammogram ± US; US of the axilla) + core (tru-cut) biopsy of the mass ± node.
qs.why: No single test is reliable alone; clinical exam + imaging + core biopsy together (triple assessment) give > 99% diagnostic accuracy.

qs.q: What is the diagnosis?
a: Breast cancer.
qs.why: A hard, fixed lump with skin changes and suspicious imaging is breast cancer until histology says otherwise.

qs.q: The radiology report shows BI-RADS 5 — what does it mean, and what do you do?
a: Highly suggestive of malignancy (≥ 95 %) → tru-cut (core) biopsy.
qs.why: BI-RADS 5 carries ≥ 95% probability of malignancy — it must be proven by core biopsy before treatment.

qs.q: Cancer confirmed — what do you want to do next?
a: Staging / metastatic work-up: CT chest-abdomen-pelvis and bone scan (+ receptor status).
qs.why: Stage decides treatment: CT chest/abdomen/pelvis and bone scan look for lung, liver and bone metastases (in large/node-positive tumours); receptor status guides systemic therapy.

qs.q: How do you treat? (by receptor status)
a: In general: surgery (breast-conserving surgery + radiotherapy, or mastectomy) + systemic therapy (chemo, hormonal, anti-HER2) + radiotherapy as indicated.
HER2+, ER/PR − (438A): one systemic + one surgical → trastuzumab (Herceptin) ± chemo + mastectomy.
HER2+, node-negative (436F): mention everything — Herceptin, (neo)adjuvant chemo, surgery (mastectomy or lumpectomy + sentinel node), radiotherapy.
Stage 3, ER/PR +, HER2 − (437A): hormonal therapy + chemotherapy + surgery (breast- conserving + radiotherapy).
Triple negative (441A/441F): neoadjuvant chemotherapy → surgery (lumpectomy or
mastectomy) with sentinel node → radiotherapy.
qs.why: Treatment = local control (surgery ± radiotherapy) + systemic therapy chosen by biology: HER2+ gets trastuzumab with chemotherapy, ER/PR+ gets hormonal therapy, large/node-positive disease often gets neoadjuvant therapy first.

qs.q: How will you check for lymph-node involvement?
a: Sentinel lymph-node biopsy (the 441A examiner focused on it).
qs.why: Sentinel node biopsy finds the first draining node — if negative, the axilla is spared a full dissection and its morbidity (lymphoedema).

qs.q: If you did a mastectomy, what else would you offer?
a: Breast reconstruction (e.g. silicone implant or autologous flap).
qs.why: Reconstruction (immediate or delayed, implant or flap) should be offered to every mastectomy patient for body image.

qs.q: What are the complications of the surgery?
a: Seroma (on the 438A checklist), wound infection, bleeding/haematoma, flap necrosis. Axillary surgery: lymphoedema, shoulder dysfunction, nerve injury — long thoracic (winged scapula), intercostobrachial (numbness).
DVT/PE.
qs.why: Raw surfaces collect fluid (seroma) and bleed; skin flaps can necrose; axillary surgery disrupts lymphatics (lymphoedema) and endangers the long thoracic and intercostobrachial nerves.

title: Breast examination
scenario: Breast examination on a manikin (there were multiple lumps in each breast). 430F
Breast examination station (check Prof. Al-Saif's tutorial). Archive

qs.q: Examine the breasts.
a: Introduce, consent, chaperone, expose to the waist; inspect sitting with hands at sides, on hips (pressing) and raised — asymmetry, skin changes, nipple changes.
Palpate lying at 45° with the arm behind the head: normal side first, all quadrants + axillary tail with flat fingers, then the nipple (discharge).
Describe any lump: site, size, shape, consistency, tenderness, mobility, fixity to skin/underlying muscle.
Examine the axillary, supraclavicular and cervical nodes; finish with the spine, abdomen (liver), lungs and arm (lymphoedema).
qs.why: Inspection in three positions shows tethering and asymmetry that only appear when the pectoral muscle contracts or the breast moves; palpation with flat fingers in all quadrants and the axillary tail, normal side first, is systematic and comparative.

extra.q: Questions the examiner may follow up with
a: What next? > 40 y → bilateral mammograms (other masses, other breast, calcifications) + bilateral US & ipsilateral axilla (cystic vs solid, vascularity) → US-guided core biopsy (histology + receptors).
If the patient is 25? → US first, then mammogram or MRI if suspicious.
DCIS → stage 0 (no CT CAP): lumpectomy + radiotherapy ± hormonal therapy. Invasive ductal carcinoma → stage it.
Mass attached to skin? → you can't pinch the skin over it. Attached to deep structures? → mobile = free; fixed = attached (test with pectoralis contracted).

title: Breast abscess / lactational mastitis
scenario: The picture/scenario showed a breast abscess with mastitis. 442B

qs.q: What do you see on physical examination?
a: Localised breast swelling, erythema and warmth, tenderness, a fluctuant mass (abscess), possible nipple discharge; check axillary nodes and systemic signs (fever, tachycardia).
qs.why: Infection gives the cardinal signs (redness, warmth, tenderness, swelling); fluctuance means pus has collected — an abscess.

qs.q: What history would you take?
a: Duration/onset of pain & swelling, fever/chills, nipple discharge, breast trauma.

Breastfeeding: currently feeding? age of baby, poor latch, cracked nipples, previous mastitis. Weight loss, night sweats, lump before the infection, skin changes; previous abscess/surgery, DM, immunosuppression; family history of breast cancer.
qs.why: Lactational infection comes from milk stasis and cracked nipples; non-lactational abscess and red flags (weight loss, prior lump) raise the possibility of an underlying cancer.
hist: Systemic signs of infection or abscess; sepsis needs urgent treatment.
Pus from the nipple supports abscess; trauma can introduce infection.
Breastfeeding, baby's age, latch, cracked nipples
Milk stasis and cracked nipples let bacteria (Staph. aureus) in — the cause of lactational mastitis.
Recurrent infection may need further evaluation.
Weight loss, night sweats, lump before the infection, skin changes
Inflammatory breast cancer can mimic an abscess and must not be missed.
Previous abscess or surgery, DM, immunosuppression
Recurrence and poor immunity predispose to abscess.
Increases the need to exclude cancer.

qs.q: What investigations would you request?
a: CBC, CRP/ESR, blood culture if septic, culture & sensitivity of aspirated pus.
Breast US (investigation of choice — distinguishes cellulitis from abscess, guides aspiration). Mammogram after resolution in older women or if malignancy suspected.
qs.why: Ultrasound tells cellulitis from abscess and guides aspiration; pus culture targets antibiotics; imaging after resolution excludes malignancy in older women.

qs.q: What is the differential diagnosis?
a: Breast abscess, acute mastitis, inflammatory breast cancer, galactocele, infected
fibroadenoma/cyst, fat necrosis.
qs.why: Inflammatory breast cancer can mimic mastitis — always keep it on the list, especially if not lactating or not responding to antibiotics.

qs.q: What is the treatment?
a: Analgesia, hydration, continue breastfeeding / empty the breast.
Antibiotics: flucloxacillin or co-amoxiclav (clindamycin if penicillin-allergic).
US-guided needle aspiration (repeat as needed); incision & drainage for large/recurrent abscesses.
Follow-up to ensure resolution and exclude malignancy.
qs.why: Staph. aureus is the usual organism (flucloxacillin); keep emptying the breast to stop stasis; pus is removed by repeated aspiration, with incision only for large/recurrent abscesses.

title: Fibroadenoma
scenario: An 18-year-old with a painless breast mass; no family history of cancer, no skin change or discharge. 439A

qs.q: What investigations will you do?
a: Ultrasound (< 35 y) ± core biopsy if indeterminate.
qs.why: Under 35 the breast is dense, so ultrasound is the imaging of choice; biopsy only if features are indeterminate.

qs.q: What is your differential diagnosis?
a: Fibroadenoma (also cyst, phyllodes tumour).
qs.why: A painless, mobile, well-defined lump in a young woman is most likely a fibroadenoma ("breast mouse"); a cyst or phyllodes tumour are the main alternatives.

qs.q: What are the indications for surgical management?
a: Large (> 3–4 cm) or progressively increasing in size (also symptomatic/patient preference, suspicious features).
qs.why: Most fibroadenomas can be left; excision for large or growing lumps (to exclude phyllodes), symptoms, suspicious features or patient choice.

qs.q: What happens if you leave it?
a: It may increase in size, remain the same, or regress.
qs.why: Fibroadenomas are hormone-responsive — about a third regress, most stay the same, and some grow.

title: Nipple discharge
scenario: A 43-year-old woman complaining of nipple discharge. (new station) 438F

qs.q: What would you ask in the history?
a: Unilateral or bilateral; spontaneous or induced; colour (bloody, serous, milky, green); painful or not; single or multiple ducts; skin changes, masses; lactating/duration of lactation; relation to the menstrual cycle; drugs; family history of breast cancer.
qs.why: The features that matter are whether it is spontaneous, unilateral, single-duct and bloody — these point to a duct lesion (papilloma or cancer) rather than physiological discharge.
hist: Bilateral discharge is usually physiological/hormonal; unilateral discharge needs investigation.
Spontaneous discharge is more significant than discharge only on squeezing.
Bloody → intraductal papilloma or cancer; milky → galactorrhoea (prolactin, drugs); green → duct ectasia; purulent → infection.
Pain suggests infection or duct ectasia.
A single duct suggests a local lesion (papilloma, cancer); multiple ducts suggest a benign cause.
Raise suspicion of an underlying cancer.
Milky discharge during or after lactation is physiological.
Hormonal (benign) causes vary with the cycle.
Antipsychotics, metoclopramide and OCP raise prolactin.

qs.q: What do you look for on examination?
a: Full breast exam: masses, skin/nipple changes (retraction, eczema — Paget's), the trigger point/duct producing discharge (single vs multiple ducts), axillary nodes; test the discharge for blood.
qs.why: Examination finds a mass, skin/nipple change (Paget's) and the trigger point that identifies the discharging duct.

qs.q: What investigations?
a: Cytology and culture of the discharge, US, mammogram, MRI, ductogram (important).
qs.why: Imaging (mammogram/US) looks for a mass; cytology and ductography/MRI locate a duct lesion and exclude cancer.

qs.q: What is the most common cause of bloody discharge?
a: Intraductal papilloma.
qs.why: A single-duct bloody discharge is usually from an intraductal papilloma (benign) — but cancer must be excluded.

qs.q: What is the most common cause of mixed (multicoloured) discharge?
a: Duct ectasia.
qs.why: Duct ectasia (dilated ducts with inspissated secretions) typically gives thick, multicoloured (green/brown) discharge from several ducts.

title: Inflammatory breast cancer
scenario: A case of inflammatory breast cancer. History, physical examination, investigations and management were asked. 439B

qs.q: What will you ask in the history?
a: Rapid onset (weeks) of a red, swollen, warm breast, often without a discrete lump; no response to antibiotics; not lactating; nipple changes; axillary swelling; constitutional & metastatic symptoms; risk factors.
qs.why: Inflammatory cancer develops fast over weeks, mimics infection, doesn't respond to antibiotics and often has no discrete lump.
hist: Rapid onset of red, swollen, warm breast
Inflammatory breast cancer develops over weeks from dermal lymphatic blockage.
Distinguishes it from typical breast cancer — the whole breast is involved.
The key clue separating it from mastitis.
Mastitis in a non-lactating woman is unusual and raises suspicion.
It often presents already advanced (stage III or IV).

qs.q: What will you find on examination?
a: Diffuse erythema & oedema involving ≥ 1/3 of the breast, peau d'orange, warmth, ± underlying mass, nipple retraction, enlarged axillary/supraclavicular nodes.
qs.why: Tumour emboli block dermal lymphatics → diffuse erythema, oedema and peau d'orange over ≥ 1/3 of the breast.

qs.q: What investigations?
a: Mammogram + US, core biopsy of the breast and skin punch biopsy (dermal lymphatic invasion), receptors; full staging (CT CAP, bone scan / PET-CT).
qs.why: Skin punch biopsy shows dermal lymphatic invasion; it is at least stage IIIB, so full staging is mandatory.

qs.q: What is the management?
a: T4d (at least stage IIIB): neoadjuvant chemotherapy (+ anti-HER2 if positive) → modified radical mastectomy (no breast-conserving surgery, no sentinel node) → post-mastectomy radiotherapy (± hormonal therapy).
qs.why: It is systemic from the outset: neoadjuvant chemotherapy first, then modified radical mastectomy (BCS and sentinel node are unreliable), then chest-wall radiotherapy.
